responses.short_answer: The thing that would actually push me to try would be a service with verifiable sourcing — something like a direct partnership with specific farms, not vague 'local supplier' language — combined with a genuinely easy pause function. What holds me back is that I already have a system I trust: Sunday at the Marché d'Aligre sets me up for the week, and I actually enjoy that process.
responses.reasoning: The core tension for me is that I don't have a convenience problem — I have a Tuesday-evening problem, when I'm tired and haven't planned well and we end up improvising or, worse, ordering something mediocre. A meal kit might solve that specific gap, but most of what I've seen is designed around the idea that people don't know how to cook, which is not my situation. The packaging also genuinely worries me: the amount of plastic and ice packs in those boxes is something I've seen friends deal with and I find it hard to justify against the environmental cost. And honestly, the subscription model itself — the way these services make cancellation deliberately opaque — is a design red flag to me professionally. I'd need to feel confident that I control the cadence completely before I'd hand over my card details.

responses.short_answer: Honnêtement, I'd pull the trigger if I found one with zero commitment — like, just let me order one box, no subscription trap. What holds me back is mainly the lock-in anxiety and the fact that half the menus I've seen look like hospital food for people who think 'spicy' means black pepper.
responses.reasoning: Look, I already use Deliveroo and Frichti on the regular, so the convenience angle isn't new to me. But every meal kit I've checked — HelloFresh, Quitoque — they all want me to commit to a weekly plan, and I already know myself: I'll forget to skip a week, get charged, and end up with a box of wilting vegetables I don't have time to use because I've got a deadline for Publicis. The thing that would actually get me is if someone did a proper collab with like a Moroccan or Japanese chef — something I'd actually be hyped to cook, not a generic 'poulet rôti aux herbes de Provence' situation. Also the app better be clean. If the UX looks like it was designed in 2011, I'm gone in ten seconds, no discussion.

responses.short_answer: Honestly, very little would make me try one. I go to the Talensac market every Saturday morning — I know the vendors, I know where my courgettes come from, and I choose what I cook based on what looks good that day. A box arriving at my door with pre-portioned ingredients and a recipe card is not cooking; it is assembly, and I am not interested in that distinction being blurred for me by clever marketing.
responses.reasoning: What holds me back is not laziness or inertia — it is a genuine disagreement with the premise. Cooking is how I decompress, how I connect with what my mother taught me, and how I control the quality of what my husband and I eat. A meal kit removes all of that and replaces it with someone else's portion sizes and sourcing decisions I cannot verify. If there were ever a scenario where I might consider it, it would have to be a sustained period of extreme professional pressure — the kind where I am working past 21h every weeknight for months — and even then I would probably turn to a good traiteur in Rezé before I subscribed to anything. The subscription model itself also troubles me: auto-renewal without clear reminders is something I find professionally and personally unacceptable.

responses.short_answer: Honestly, I'd try it tomorrow if they could guarantee big enough portions and a delivery slot that doesn't make me wait around like an idiot. What holds me back is the fine print on these subscriptions — I don't want some service billing me every week forever because I forgot to click 'pause.'
responses.reasoning: Look, after a full day pulling cable and climbing around in people's attics, the last thing I want is to drive to Leclerc and figure out what to cook. My wife and I — we eat well, we eat a lot. Me especially. So if a meal kit shows up with some tiny 'deux personnes parisiennes' portion that leaves me hungry at 9pm, that's straight in the bin. What I'd love is to find something with a bit of Caribbean inspiration — a colombo, a court-bouillon de poisson — something that teaches me a new trick for the weekend grill. But every time I look at these services online, there's always some asterisk: 'cancel anytime*' and then the asterisk sends you to a paragraph I'd need a lawyer to decode. That makes me nervous. Not because I can't afford it, but because I hate feeling like I've been played.

responses.short_answer: If I found a service that let me choose a delivery day that actually works with my shift schedule, had genuinely kid-friendly recipes — not just 'mild' versions of things my kids still won't touch — and let me skip weeks without fees, I'd subscribe tomorrow. What holds me back is mostly the delivery timing and the fear of paying for vegetables that end up in the bin because I got called in for an extra shift.
responses.reasoning: I work rotating shifts at Necker, so a Tuesday delivery could be perfect one week and a complete disaster the next. I've looked at a few services — HelloFresh, Marmiton à la carte — and the flexible skipping is always fine print. Also, my daughter is six and has very specific texture issues, and my son is four and goes through phases where he refuses anything green. I've read enough on these services to know the recipes are adult-calibrated even when they say 'famille.' And honestly, the food waste anxiety is real — I already feel guilty when a bunch of coriander goes brown in the fridge. A kit that promises fresh produce for five meals when I might only cook three? That math makes me nervous. If someone could genuinely solve the schedule flexibility and prove the recipes work for actual children, not just children in marketing photos, I would be a loyal customer.

responses.short_answer: To try one of these services, I would need to see a clear, verifiable cost comparison against what I already spend at Carrefour or the market — portions for five people, not two adults with a garnish. What holds me back is primarily the pricing structure and the subscription mechanism, which in my experience is designed to be easy to enter and inconvenient to leave.
responses.reasoning: I have looked at a couple of these services — HelloFresh was advertised on the back of a magazine we had at home — and the per-meal pricing, once you calculate it for a family of five, is simply not competitive with a well-managed weekly shop. My wife and I already plan meals on Sunday, we grow some of our own vegetables on the allotment, and I have no interest in paying a premium for someone else to portion out carrots and wrap them in plastic. What might change my assessment is a genuine trial offer with no automatic renewal, recipes that are straightforward enough that the older children can participate, and a realistic family-sized option. The risk I cannot accept is signing up, receiving one or two deliveries that the children reject because the recipes are too elaborate, and then spending forty-five minutes on the phone trying to cancel a contract.

responses.short_answer: What would finally push me to try one is finding a service that actually includes West African recipes — real ones, with proper ingredients — combined with genuinely transparent cancellation terms and verified sourcing. What holds me back is that every service I've looked at treats 'diversity' as adding a Thai curry once a month, and I have no interest in paying a premium to cook food I can already find on any French supermarket shelf.
responses.reasoning: I cook thieboudienne and yassa for my daughter on weekends — that is not incidental, that is intentional. It is how I transmit something to her. So when I evaluate a meal kit, my first question is: does this service see me as a customer, or does it assume I want a slightly fancier version of what's already in the Intermarché? I've done enough reading to know that most subscription models in France are designed with friction — the trial price is attractive, the cancellation flow is deliberately obscure. I would need to see actual contract terms, not a landing page promise of 'pause anytime.' And the packaging situation is a serious problem: I've seen services ship a single lime in its own plastic tray and label it 'eco-responsible.' That is not a detail I overlook.

responses.short_answer: Honestly? A genuinely affordable single-serving option with no subscription lock-in would probably push me over the edge — something like 10-15€ for one meal that actually teaches me *why* I'm doing each step, not just what to do. What holds me back is that every service I've looked at seems calibrated for like... a couple in a spacious kitchen with a well-stocked pantry, which is the precise opposite of my situation.
responses.reasoning: My stipend as a doctoral researcher is, let's say, not optimized for discretionary spending — Paris rent takes a significant chunk and I'm already doing a kind of resource allocation that would make a behavioral economist wince. I've genuinely researched meal kit options because I approach cooking the same way I approach a new protocol in the lab: I want to understand the underlying mechanisms, not just follow steps blindly. But when I see services charging 50 or 60 euros a week for two people, I just... close the tab, because that's not even a realistic experimental condition for my budget. What would actually convert me is a pay-as-you-go model where I could order one kit when I have a free Sunday evening — because my lab schedule is completely unpredictable and committing to a weekly delivery feels like setting myself up for anxiety and food waste, which honestly stresses me out more than the cost.

responses.short_answer: Honestly, probably nothing would get me to try one — or at least nothing any of these services currently offer. A genuinely commitment-free, single-order option with decent ingredients might get me to test it once, out of mild curiosity. But I'd expect to be disappointed.
responses.reasoning: I already go to the Victor Hugo market on Saturdays and the whole point of cooking for me is choosing the ingredients myself — not receiving a bag of pre-weighed leek batons and a laminated card telling me what to feel. The subscription model is designed to make cancellation painful, and I've read enough dark pattern complaints to know how that story ends. What holds me back is mostly that the product is solving a problem I don't have, while creating several I'd find genuinely irritating.

responses.short_answer: What would tip me toward trying one is finding a service that offers genuine portions for one or two people, with a transparent subscription structure I can pause or cancel without navigating a labyrinth. What holds me back, frankly, is that I have not yet seen one that seems designed for someone like me — and the few I have looked at online felt as though they were aimed at a young couple in Paris who photographs their dinner.
responses.reasoning: I am at a stage where cooking for one — or occasionally for a friend — is genuinely new territory after nearly twenty years of feeding a household. The practical argument for a meal kit is real: I do not always want to buy a full bunch of leeks when I need two. But I read the fine print before I commit to anything, and the cancellation conditions I have seen described — automatic renewal, minimum weeks, credits rather than refunds — are exactly the kind of arrangement I refuse to walk into without full clarity. Beyond the contractual concern, there is a quality question. I buy my tomatoes at the Tuesday market in Schiltigheim and I know what a good one feels like; I am not convinced a cardboard box arriving from a warehouse can match that. It would take a service with verifiable sourcing, a genuine pause function, and the decency to speak to me as an adult who cooks — not as someone who needs enthusiasm and emojis to get through a recipe.
